History: reporting conditions and measuring variation
A language-model score without its input conditions and scope does not identify what was evaluated or establish which capabilities were checked.
Model Cards for Model Reporting was presented in 2019. Mitchell and colleagues propose model documentation that includes intended uses and evaluation conditions; a model card is not itself proof of quality.
Model Cards describe evaluation conditions and intended uses; later fine-tuning experiments study variation across initializations and data orders. Reporting scope and measuring variation answer different questions.
In Fine-Tuning Pretrained Language Models: Weight Initializations, Data Orders, and Early Stopping, published in 2020, Dodge and colleagues study fine-tuning variability associated with initialization and data order for pretrained language models. This does not measure variability in the course’s tiny decoder.
Keep a fixed regression reference when changing an LLM pipeline, while recording separately the evidence needed for quality, seed sensitivity and hardware claims.
The Rust reporting contrast uses the same observation. Reading only the mean NLL with this expression gives a number:
trace .observation() .final_evaluation() .decoder() .mean_nll()
trace.report() also states the evaluation unit, input identity, replay accounting and limits. It does not retrain a historical model or execute a seed sweep.

reading.value:
The problem: changes need a fixed comparison point
The final chapter of LLM from scratch joined the tokenizer, decoder, training, evaluation, checkpoint and generation code. This practical course starts from a separate copy of that implementation. If the data, configuration and code change together, a changed result no longer tells you which version you observed. You need a fixed reference that identifies its inputs and states exactly what its checks establish.
This chapter runs the completed first-course pipeline without modifying it. The practical copy can then evolve while this comparison point stays fixed. The example gives that reference an input identity and a report whose claims stay attached to their evidence. The identity identifies the fixed inputs. The checks establish which behavior this execution reproduced. Neither establishes useful laptop-scale capability.
What the reference actually does
The fixture assigns 8 documents to training, 2 to validation and 2 to test. The decoder has 1188 learned scalar parameters and context capacity 4 tokens. Its primary training schedule and separately executed replay each perform 32 updates on full batches of 16 windows, with 4 valid targets per window. Therefore, each schedule consumes
32\cdot16\cdot4=2048

valid training targets. One pipeline invocation includes both schedules: 4096 targets altogether. These counts are derived from the frozen full-batch schedule, not from a new runtime token counter. Evaluation targets and generated tokens are separate quantities.
The report’s independent_schedules field counts two separately executed copies of the same schedule from training seed 39, not statistically independent seed samples.
The replay agrees bit for bit with the primary training result in this execution. The selected decoder and frozen bigram then score the same 1744 overlapping test-window target slots. Their mean negative log-likelihoods are approximately 3.866087547 and 3.981342714 nats per slot, respectively. This known comparison is a regression check: rerunning it can expose changes in the checked behavior. It is not an independent estimate of generalization.
There are only 442 within-document transition occurrences in those test documents. Overlapping windows repeat occurrences, so 1744 is not a count of distinct transitions. A separate policy would score each occurrence once, using the longest available causal prefix capped at four tokens and only its newest-position distribution. This run does not report numeric mean NLL or perplexity under that policy.
The checkpoint round trip preserves its encoded bytes, model and optimizer bits, and tokenizer. The restored decoder reproduces logits for the fixed At probe, encoded as token IDs [67,118]. Cached and complete-prefix generation agree on token IDs [260,34,34]: Cyrillic т followed by two spaces. Agreement checks the two generation paths; those three tokens do not demonstrate useful language quality.

The solution: identify inputs, then interpret evidence
R_{\mathrm{ref}}=\operatorname{SHA256}(\mathrm{config}_{1188}\Vert\mathrm{fixture}\Vert\mathrm{source\_revision})

The identity’s symbols and fixed settings
R_{\mathrm{ref}} is a 256-bit digest, displayed as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Its three named inputs are:
\mathrm{config}_{1188}: a canonical record of eighteen tiny-run settings, together with the invariant that the decoder has 1188 parameters. \mathrm{fixture}: a canonical record of SHA-256 digests of the exact corpus bytes and exact split-manifest bytes. Even a byte change that leaves parsed JSON meaning unchanged creates a different input identity. \mathrm{source\_revision}: a verified source identity combining a baseline revision with the exact forty Rust source files of the completed first-course crate, including its module declarations in lib.rs.
Here \Vert means composition into the shared identity format’s named, canonical fields, not writing three unframed strings beside one another. That distinction matters: without field boundaries, different input sequences can have the same concatenated bytes. The helper orders fields, serializes one unambiguous record and hashes its complete bytes.
The settings fix eight BPE merges; decoder width, feed-forward width and context capacity of four; one attention head and one block; stride one; training and evaluation batch sizes of sixteen and one hundred twenty-eight; thirty-two updates; learning rate 0.04; gradient-norm cap 1; training seed 39; generation seed 38; bigram smoothing 1; generation temperature 0.8; top-k four; and three generated tokens. The identity records floating-point settings by their exact bit patterns rather than rounded display text.

That call already includes primary training and full replay. pub fn run_reference_handoff( corpus_source: &str, split_source: &str, checkpoint_path: impl AsRef<Path>, source: &ReferenceSourceProof, ) -> Result<ReferenceHandoffTrace, ReferenceHandoffError> { if sha256(corpus_source.as_bytes()).as_hex() != CORPUS_SHA256 { return Err(ReferenceHandoffError::FixtureMismatch("corpus")); } if sha256(split_source.as_bytes()).as_hex() != SPLITS_SHA256 { return Err(ReferenceHandoffError::FixtureMismatch("split manifest")); } // Safe callers obtain this opaque proof only through the foundation's // approved-manifest/compiled-census verification, not a revision string. let identity = reference_input_identity( &tiny_config_identity()?, corpus_source.as_bytes(), split_source.as_bytes(), source.identity(), )?; let digest = identity.digest()?; let observation = run_capstone( corpus_source, split_source, checkpoint_path, CapstoneConfig::tiny(), )?; let evaluation = observation.final_evaluation(); let checkpoint = observation.checkpoint(); if observation.training().parameter_count() != 1188 || observation.training().optimizer_step() != 32 || !observation.training().replay_bitwise() || evaluation.window_count() != 436 || evaluation.window_target_slot_count() != 1744 || evaluation.document_transition_occurrence_count() != 442 || !evaluation.decoder().mean_nll().is_finite() || !evaluation.bigram().mean_nll().is_finite() || !checkpoint.bytes_roundtrip() || !checkpoint.model_bits_exact() || !checkpoint.optimizer_bits_exact() || !checkpoint.tokenizer_exact() || !checkpoint.prompt_logits_bitwise() || !observation.generation().tokens_exact() || !observation.generation().decisions_bitwise() || !observation.generation().rng_state_exact() { return Err(ReferenceHandoffError::Invariant( "scalar reference handoff evidence changed", )); } Ok(ReferenceHandoffTrace { identity, digest, source_revision: source.source_revision().to_owned(), observation, }) }
What matching identities do not prove
A matching digest identifies the same canonical input record, subject to the hash’s collision-resistance assumption. It does not prove that the algorithm is correct or that a new machine will reproduce every floating-point bit.
The source identity deliberately covers the forty first-course source files, not the evolving practical crate, this chapter’s reporting wrapper or interface. Toolchain, locked dependencies and arithmetic environment are recorded separately. A matching source digest is therefore not evidence that two execution environments match. The temporary checkpoint path is also outside the input identity; changing that path does not change the model’s fixed inputs.
Likewise, exact checkpoint reload is narrower than complete job resumption. This check does not restore every data cursor, in-flight operation or whole-job continuation state. No laptop throughput is measured here.

Formula: distinguish retention from quality
For a nonempty input corpus, the final document-retention fraction is
r_{\mathrm{keep}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{prepared}}}{N_{\mathrm{input}}}

Here N_{\mathrm{input}} is the number of input document occurrences, N_{\mathrm{prepared}} is the number remaining after the declared preparation stages, and r_{\mathrm{keep}} is a dimensionless fraction. Neither count is a byte count or token count. With zero input documents, the fraction is undefined; report that condition rather than inventing a zero-quality score.
In the six-document example, quality filtering retains 4/6 of the original input. Duplicate removal retains 3/4 of its own input: the four records that reached that stage. Their product is the final retention fraction,
\frac{4}{6}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}.

Changing the denominator changes the question. Reporting 1/6 as the duplicate stage’s exclusion fraction would use the original input population rather than the 4 records the duplicate stage examined. Keep every stage’s entering and leaving document counts so its fraction can be interpreted locally.
Keeping half the input says how much remains under this policy. It does not say that half was bad, that the survivors are safe, or that a model trained on them will perform well. Those claims need different evidence.

History: more text was not the whole solution
Collecting readable text alone does not document its intended use, control the weight of repeated occurrences or protect held-out evaluation from training overlap.
Dataset documentation makes source context reviewable; deduplication studies connect repeated training text with memorization and train-test overlap in their measured settings.
Datasheets for Datasets was first posted in 2018. Gebru and colleagues propose documenting dataset motivation, composition, collection and intended uses so those choices can be reviewed. Documentation records context; it does not itself establish permission or privacy.
The 2021 C4 analysis examined where web-corpus text came from and what filtering removed. Its finding that blocklist filtering disproportionately excluded text from and about minority individuals is a reason to inspect exclusions, not to label every filter neutral.
In 2022, Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better studied duplicate handling in training corpora. Lee and colleagues report reduced memorized output and train-test overlap after deduplication in their studied corpora and models; those outcomes are not measurements of this course fixture. They explain why duplicate handling and evaluation separation matter in addition to collecting and documenting text.
The following Rust comparison loads two identical supplied records and keeps both. It illustrates the limitation of merely reading raw occurrences, not a reimplementation of those studies’ preparation tools:
Reading two identical JSONL records returns two documents; the loader does not silently perform duplicate removal. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#loading-is-not-preparation #[test] fn loader_does_not_curate_repeated_ids_or_text() { let source = b"{\"id\":\"same\",\"text\":\"same text\"}\n{\"id\":\"same\",\"text\":\"same text\"}\n"; let documents = PreparedCorpusReader::new(Cursor::new(source), limits()) .unwrap() .collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>() .unwrap(); assert_eq!(documents.len(), 2); assert_eq!(documents[0], documents[1]); }
Keep documented source and selection evidence, inspect exclusions, handle related records together and preserve held-out roles before tokenizer learning or model training. No single preparation statistic certifies suitability.

Load the prepared output in Rust
PreparedCorpusReader accepts any caller-supplied BufRead stream. A file, memory buffer or database export can supply that stream without changing the loader. Standard buffered I/O reads physical lines; Serde JSON parses their objects. The loader preserves decoded text and metadata. It does not normalize text, reject duplicate content or assign a split.
The prepared-corpus loader uses Serde JSON to decode required document fields, then rejects blank IDs or text without rewriting their content. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#prepared-document-json let document: PreparedDocument = serde_json::from_slice(&self.buffer) .map_err(|source| CorpusReadError::InvalidJson { line, source })?; for (field, value) in [("id", &document.id), ("text", &document.text)] { if value.trim().is_empty() { return Err(CorpusReadError::EmptyField { line, field }); } }
The caller chooses maximum source-record bytes, document count and cumulative decoded-text bytes. Record bytes include the physical line ending; decoded text bytes count the UTF-8 representation of the text value, not JSON syntax or metadata. An oversized record, malformed JSON, missing required field, failed read or exceeded limit stops the stream with an error. No failed document is returned or counted. Documents returned earlier are not rolled back.
The prepared-corpus iterator stops after successful end of input or its first error; it never resumes past a failed record. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#prepared-corpus-stream fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> { if self.finished { return None; } match self.read_document() { Ok(Some(document)) => Some(Ok(document)), Ok(None) => { self.finished = true; None } Err(error) => { self.finished = true; Some(Err(error)) } } }
The demo reads standard input, retains only the first three document descriptions for its summary, and emits that summary only after the complete input succeeds. It can therefore inspect a large stream without retaining every text. This is not a transactional storage adapter: a caller storing documents as they arrive must provide its own staging if partial results must stay unpublished.
The Rust demo loads supplied prepared documents, reports their count and decoded text bytes, and does not repeat NeMo's preparation operations. rust/demos/practical-ch02-corpus-preparation/src/lib.rs#load-prepared-corpus pub fn summarize<R: BufRead>( source: R, limits: ReadLimits, ) -> Result<CorpusSummary, CorpusReadError> { let mut documents = PreparedCorpusReader::new(source, limits)?; let mut first_documents = Vec::with_capacity(SUMMARY_DOCUMENTS); for document in documents.by_ref() { let document = document?; if first_documents.len() < SUMMARY_DOCUMENTS { first_documents.push(DocumentSummary { id: document.id, metadata_fields: document.metadata.keys().cloned().collect(), text_utf8_bytes: document.text.len(), }); } // The tokenizer can consume document.text here. This chapter only loads // prepared records; no preparation operation is repeated inside Rust. } Ok(CorpusSummary { first_documents, loaded: documents.progress(), }) }

Practical preparation with NeMo Curator
This workflow uses a separately built NeMo Curator image. You need Linux, Docker, a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so Docker can expose the GPU. The pinned NeMo release must be compatible with that CUDA/driver stack. Rust’s prepared-corpus reader does not require a GPU or CUDA.
Run the following commands from the repository root. The image build may use network access to obtain the external tool. It does not acquire a training corpus or add NeMo to the Rust/site image:
docker build --file docker/nemo-curator.Dockerfile \ --tag learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 .
With the NeMo image built and the NVIDIA GPU available to Docker, run from the repository root. Create a fresh output directory for the exercise, then run the tool with network access disabled. The read-only mount supplies the recipe and its six-record fixture; the writable mount receives generated preparation output:
mkdir -p .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture docker run --rm --network none --gpus all --memory=8g --cpus=2 --shm-size=1g \ --hostname course-nemo --add-host course-nemo:127.0.0.1 \ --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/tools/nemo-curator",target=/course,readonly \ --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/.build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture",target=/output \ learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 \ /course/prepare_corpus.py \ --input /course/fixtures/raw.jsonl --output /output \ --split-policy /course/fixtures/splits.json
Use an empty output directory. If the directory already contains an earlier attempt, choose a different directory rather than overwriting its evidence. The hostname mapping lets the local Ray workers resolve their container on loopback; it does not enable external network access.
The recipe invokes NeMo’s reader, configured word-count filter, exact duplicate identification and duplicate-removal workflow. Identification produces IDs to remove; it is not already the prepared text. The removal workflow must consume those IDs from the same input and ID policy, then export the remaining documents.
The filter configuration in tools/nemo-curator/prepare_corpus.py uses the library’s pipeline and stages; the recipe does not implement its own filter:
Pipeline( name="course_corpus_quality", stages=[ JsonlReader(file_paths=str(input_path), read_kwargs=read_kwargs), ScoreFilter( filter_obj=WordCountFilter(min_words=min_words, max_words=max_words, lang="en"), score_field="word_count", ), JsonlWriter(path=str(quality_path), mode="error"), ], ).run(executor=executor)
The surrounding recipe supplies the reader settings, starts a local Ray client, and runs NeMo’s exact-identification and text-removal workflows. The defaults set min_words to 3 and max_words to 20. Command-line options change those values; retain them with the output report when comparing different policies. The supplied split-policy file is independent of the observed scores.
Inspect the generated report and exported files with these commands, still from the repository root:
cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/report.json cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/prepared.jsonl cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/train.jsonl
For this fixture, the expected stage counts are 6 input documents, 4 after word-count filtering and 3 after exact duplicate removal. The final texts are A cat naps., A dog runs. and Rain feeds trees.; do not require one particular cat-story ID. The report also records one document in each role. prepared.jsonl contains all three documents for inspection; train.jsonl, validation.jsonl and test.jsonl contain their respective selections and retain the split metadata.
This is a tiny execution example with a fixed assignment of known source groups. It is not an approval of a larger corpus, a privacy check, proof that all related groups were found or a trained-model result. The helper limits input to 4 MiB and 4096 documents by default so the example is inspectable; those are not a recipe for processing the previously acquired large corpus. A bulk run needs its own feasible configuration and complete selection evidence.
For a real corpus, also retain input provenance, the tool version and configuration, excluded-document counts, the duplicate policy, split assignments and the scope of overlap and privacy review. A successful small fixture does not establish that the same resource settings fit a larger dataset. Select and measure that workload separately, preserving the raw inputs and every failed attempt.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value:
The problem: the model learns from the text we let through
A language model learns to predict tokens from the documents supplied during training. Its optimizer does not decide whether those documents are appropriate for the task, whether we may use them, or whether a purportedly unseen test example also appears in the training input. Those decisions must happen before training.
Repeated text creates another problem. If one training pass visits every stored document occurrence, each copy of a document supplies another copy of its token targets. The repeated text receives more influence without adding new examples. Removing duplicates changes that weighting; it does not merely save disk space.
Corpus preparation therefore has two outputs: selected text and evidence about how it was selected. We need source context, declared exclusion rules, duplicate handling and protected evaluation boundaries. A large file or a successful download supplies none of those conclusions on its own.
We will use NVIDIA NeMo Curator to prepare text. It is an external tool, not part of the Rust language model, and another preparation tool can replace it if it produces the same documented input for the model. Rust will only load the prepared documents. The extended tokenizer in Chapter 3 will then learn from the training documents, not the validation or test documents.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value:
The solution: prepare documents, then load a stable format
Keep one document as one record throughout the preparation pipeline. Retain a stable document ID and the source information needed to trace that record. A source record should identify where the text came from, its revision and the applicable license and attribution. A checksum identifies selected bytes; it does not establish permission to use those bytes or tell us what they contain.
Apply declared quality rules, inspect what those rules exclude, and handle duplicates before final training input is frozen. Quality rules are proxies: for example, a minimum word count rejects short records, not every unsuitable record. A rule can also remove useful text. Inspect both survivors and exclusions rather than interpreting a low exclusion rate as success.
Keep privacy review separate from quality scoring. Passing a word-count filter or removing duplicates does not remove names, addresses, credentials or other sensitive content. Withhold unresolved records from training; do not copy their sensitive text into public reports. Retain enough source and transformation information to identify affected derived corpora if an input is withdrawn. Removing a source from a later corpus does not erase what an already trained model may have learned from it.
A six-document example
The practical example uses course-authored text, not a result for a large training corpus. Its JSONL input contains these six documents:
Document ID | Text | Source group | Relevant observation story-a | A cat naps. | family-a | Three words story-b | A cat naps. | family-a | An identical copy of story-a story-c | A dog runs. | family-b | Three words story-d | Rain feeds trees. | family-c | Three words story-e | hi | family-e | One word story-f | !!! | family-f | Punctuation only
Configure NeMo’s word-count filter to retain records with at least 3 and at most 20 words. Its English setting counts whitespace-separated items; that proxy is not a linguistic definition of a word. The 4 story occurrences survive; hi and the punctuation-only record do not. Exact duplicate removal then leaves 3 distinct story texts. The punctuation-only record has one whitespace-separated item too; this particular rule rejects it for length, not because it recognizes punctuation as unsuitable language-model training text. The duplicate-removal workflow may retain either cat-story ID; the result we care about here is one cat-story occurrence, not a promised representative ID or output-file order.
Before deduplication, the cat story occupies 2 of the 4 surviving document occurrences. After deduplication, it occupies 1 of 3 distinct documents. Under uniform sampling of these whole-stage document occurrences before separating their roles, its selection probability would change from 2/4 to 1/3. That calculation illustrates duplicate weighting, not a sampler used to train on this fixture. Actual token-target weighting also depends on document length, split selection and the batching policy; document fractions are not token fractions.
NeMo’s exact method groups hashes of text and identifies copies to remove. It does not identify paraphrases, and hash grouping is not an adversarial collision-proof comparison. NeMo’s fuzzy method uses approximate similarity search for near-duplicates. Its configuration trades missed matches against unwanted matches; it does not certify a universal similarity cutoff or detect all ways an evaluation example could have leaked into training.
Freeze the roles of the prepared documents
The training split supplies examples for fitting the tokenizer and model. The validation split supplies examples for selecting settings or deciding when to stop training. The test split is reserved for final evaluation. Do not move a difficult held-out document into training after seeing its score.
Related records must not be scattered across those roles. Treat an identified duplicate family or other known related source group as one unit when assigning splits. Otherwise two different IDs can put substantially the same example in both training and evaluation. For this fixture, the two cat-story copies share family-a; their different IDs do not make them independent examples.
For the exercise, a supplied policy assigns family-a, family-e and family-f to training, family-b to validation and family-c to test. We fix that policy before running the filters. Both cat-story copies therefore have the same role regardless of which ID duplicate removal keeps. The prepared fixture has one document in each role: the cat story in training, the dog story in validation and the rain story in test.
The recipe uses Pandas to join those declared assignments to the source-group metadata. It refuses an unassigned group rather than choosing a convenient role after seeing the output. This checks the supplied groups, not whether we have discovered every related pair. One held-out story is also far too little evidence for a meaningful model-quality estimate.
Split disjointness and decontamination are different checks. Disjoint IDs do not prove different text. Removing exact duplicates does not prove that near-copies or external benchmark examples are absent. Declare the protected evaluation material and the overlap method before inspecting results, report its measured scope, and keep unresolved overlaps out of training. A check against a named evaluation set does not establish internet-wide contamination freedom.
Export documents, not preparation-specific objects
The handoff to Rust is UTF-8 JSON Lines: one JSON object per physical line. Each object has a nonblank string id and a nonblank string text. Other fields are retained as metadata. For example:
{"id":"story-c","text":"A dog runs.","source_group":"family-b"}
The document ID is a label, not a token ID or a required filename. The text is still text; tokenization comes next. A newline inside document text must be escaped as \n inside the JSON string, so it does not create a second record. Source and split records remain linked to the exported documents, but a JSONL file alone does not certify that those decisions were made correctly.

# Chapter 0: The structure of Practical LLM in Rust

<!-- contract-section:scope -->
## Scope

Orientation only: identify the independent copied implementation, prerequisites,
initial material and later roadmap. Do not introduce a second algorithm, formula
lesson, Rust implementation sample, exercise, answer or cheat sheet.

<!-- contract-section:overview -->
## Orientation commitments

The practical crate starts from the restored first-course implementation and is
evolved independently. First-course lessons and algorithms stay unchanged.
Chapter 1 records the fixed baseline experiment; Chapter 2 separates external
preparation from Rust loading; Chapter 3 extends the existing BPE implementation.
Available links must correspond to published practical chapters. If Chapter 3
is pending at the foundation checkpoint, show its named role as roadmap text
until its complete chapter is published.

<!-- contract-section:history -->
## Starting point

The historical comparison for this orientation is course-local: building small
mechanisms first, then extending the completed model. Make no new primary-source
historical claim and reuse no first-course diagram as a new taught mechanism.

<!-- contract-section:course-path -->
## Chapter sequence

Give each initial chapter its concrete purpose: identified reference inputs and
scope, external preparation and Rust loading, then extension of existing BPE.
Link available practical Chapters 1 and 2; name Chapter 3's role and link the
course index for current availability. Explain the subsequent batching, model
configuration, GPU, training, resume, evaluation, adaptation, inference and
serving stages as a roadmap rather than completed measurements.

<!-- contract-section:visualization -->
## Navigation evidence

An ordered list supplies the chapter-to-purpose mapping. No figure is required.
Explain that concrete reason without referring to rendering or build machinery.

<!-- contract-section:decoder-connection -->
## Practical path

Keep one causal text model as the subject. Distinguish small examples from
full-corpus or hardware measurements. CPU reference and loading of prepared
documents remain available; the GPU-backed path and external NeMo stack require
a compatible NVIDIA device and driver.

<!-- contract-section:localization -->
## Locale scope

Practical lessons are English only, including order zero; locale configuration
and future activation remain supported. Russian home may link explicitly to the
English practical destination. No Russian practical lesson is emitted.

<!-- contract-section:acceptance -->
## Acceptance

Scoped orientation schema, no cheat sheet, static links and locale semantics,
English independent reviews and adjudications, and sole-Firefox desktop/narrow
containment and navigation. The foundation checkpoint retains pending full-data
preparation and hardware gates; small fixtures do not discharge them.

{/* chapter-section:overview */}

## Start from a working model

This course starts from a working language model and studies what must change as
the data, model and workload grow. The starting implementation is a separate
copy of the model completed in *LLM from scratch*. It already contains byte-pair
tokenization, tensors, automatic differentiation, a causal decoder, training,
evaluation, checkpoints and cached generation. Here we extend those parts.

Chapter 0 is an orientation. Chapter 1 begins the learning material by recording
exactly what the small reference model demonstrates. That record gives later
changes a concrete comparison point.

## Before starting

Complete [LLM from scratch](/en/course/) or bring equivalent experience with
Rust, byte-pair encoding, causal attention, gradients and next-token training.
The first course's [Chapter 39](/en/course/39-end-to-end-llm/) shows the complete
small model. Familiarity with that model matters more than memorizing its
chapter numbers.

The initial reference and Rust loading of an already prepared corpus run on a
CPU. The GPU-backed practical path requires a compatible NVIDIA GPU. The external
corpus-preparation example uses NVIDIA NeMo Curator and needs a GPU and driver
compatible with its pinned CUDA/RAPIDS environment. NeMo prepares text outside
the Rust model; another tool can supply the same prepared-document format.

{/* chapter-section:history */}

## Keep the completed model as the starting point

The first course builds the mechanisms of a small causal language model. This
course begins with its completed implementation and studies how data handling,
execution, training and inference must change for larger workloads. The Rust
implementation for this course lives in
`rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical`. Its examples extend that copy; the first
course keeps its own implementation.

{/* chapter-section:course-path */}

## Follow the practical path

1. [Chapter 1: Record the reference model](../01-reference-core-handoff/) binds
   the tiny experiment to its inputs and separates repeatable results from
   claims about language quality or speed.
2. [Chapter 2: Prepare a corpus](../02-corpus-preparation/) separates external
   text preparation from Rust loading, and preserves document and split identity.
3. Chapter 3 extends byte-pair encoding. It adds
   bounded ingestion, local pair updates and efficient application of frozen
   merge ranks to the existing tokenizer.

The [practical course index](/en/practical-llm-in-rust/) links to the lessons
currently available. The later curriculum continues with variable-length batches and packing,
configurable decoder depth and shape, GPU execution, larger training runs,
complete resume state, evaluation, adaptation, quantized inference and serving.
These are stages of one causal text model. Their examples become available as
each mechanism is implemented and measured.

## Read the examples at their stated scale

Small fixtures make intermediate values inspectable: a pair count, a token
sequence, a loss or a restored state. They establish the behavior shown for
those inputs. They do not establish full-corpus throughput, useful generated
language, or a larger model's memory use. Full-data runs and hardware
measurements supply that separate evidence.

{/* chapter-section:visualization */}

## Use the sequence to navigate

An ordered chapter list connects each available lesson to its purpose and names
the later stages. The individual lessons introduce diagrams where a computation
or comparison benefits from one.

{/* chapter-section:decoder-connection */}

## Continue with the reference experiment

Corpus preparation and tokenization supply the causal decoder's inputs. Later
chapters change how that same model is configured, trained, evaluated and used
for generation. Start by establishing the reference experiment in
[Chapter 1](../01-reference-core-handoff/).

Separate checks observe replay, fixed-window evaluation, reload and cached generation. Neither the identity nor those checks establishes useful language quality, complete job resumption or laptop throughput.",
  inputs: "Identify the fixed inputs",
  checks: "Read the checked reference behavior",
  future: "Keep unmeasured capabilities separate",
  digest: "SHA-256 identity of the fixed input record",
  parameters: "Learned scalar parameters",
  slots: "Overlapping test-window target slots",
  transitions: "Within-document transition occurrences",
  generation: "Generated token IDs",
  limits: "Not established: useful language quality, complete job resumption or laptop throughput.",

{/* chapter-section:worked-example */}

## The problem: changes need a fixed comparison point

The final chapter of *LLM from scratch* joined the tokenizer, decoder, training,
evaluation, checkpoint and generation code. This practical course starts from a
separate copy of that implementation. If the
data, configuration and code change together, a changed result no longer tells
you which version you observed. You need a fixed reference that identifies its
inputs and states exactly what its checks establish.

This chapter runs the completed first-course pipeline without modifying it. The
practical copy can then evolve while this comparison point stays fixed. The example gives that reference
an input identity and a report whose claims stay attached to their evidence.
The identity identifies the fixed inputs. The checks establish which behavior
this execution reproduced. Neither establishes useful laptop-scale capability.

### What the reference actually does

The fixture assigns $8$ documents to training, $2$ to validation and $2$ to test.
The decoder has $1188$ learned scalar parameters and context capacity $4$ tokens.
Its primary training schedule and separately executed replay each perform $32$ updates
on full batches of $16$ windows, with $4$ valid targets per window. Therefore,
each schedule consumes

$$
32\cdot16\cdot4=2048
$$

valid training targets. One pipeline invocation includes both schedules: $4096$
targets altogether. These counts are derived from the frozen full-batch
schedule, not from a new runtime token counter. Evaluation targets and generated
tokens are separate quantities.

The report's `independent_schedules` field counts two separately executed copies
of the same schedule from training seed $39$, not statistically independent
seed samples.

The replay agrees bit for bit with the primary training result in this
execution. The selected decoder and frozen bigram then score the same $1744$
overlapping test-window target slots. Their mean negative log-likelihoods are
approximately $3.866087547$ and $3.981342714$ nats per slot, respectively.
This known comparison is a regression check: rerunning it can expose changes
in the checked behavior. It is not an independent estimate of generalization.

There are only $442$ within-document transition occurrences in those test
documents. Overlapping windows repeat occurrences, so $1744$ is not a count
of distinct transitions. A separate policy would score each occurrence once,
using the longest available causal prefix capped at four tokens and only its
newest-position distribution. This run does not report numeric mean NLL or
perplexity under that policy.

The checkpoint round trip preserves its encoded bytes, model and optimizer
bits, and tokenizer. The restored decoder reproduces logits for the fixed
`At` probe, encoded as token IDs `[67,118]`. Cached and complete-prefix generation
agree on token IDs `[260,34,34]`: Cyrillic `т` followed by two spaces. Agreement
checks the two generation paths; those three tokens do not demonstrate useful
language quality.

{/* chapter-section:formula */}

## The solution: identify inputs, then interpret evidence

$$
R_{\mathrm{ref}}=\operatorname{SHA256}(\mathrm{config}_{1188}\Vert\mathrm{fixture}\Vert\mathrm{source\_revision})
$$

{/* chapter-section:symbol-glossary */}

## The identity's symbols and fixed settings

$R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is a $256$-bit digest, displayed as $64$ lowercase hexadecimal
characters. Its three named inputs are:

- $\mathrm{config}_{1188}$: a canonical record of eighteen tiny-run settings,
  together with the invariant that the decoder has $1188$ parameters.
- $\mathrm{fixture}$: a canonical record of SHA-256 digests of the exact corpus
  bytes and exact split-manifest bytes. Even a byte change that leaves parsed
  JSON meaning unchanged creates a different input identity.
- $\mathrm{source\_revision}$: a verified source identity combining a baseline
  revision with the exact forty Rust source files of the completed first-course
  crate, including its module declarations in `lib.rs`.

Here $\Vert$ means composition into the shared identity format's named,
canonical fields, not writing three unframed strings beside one another.
That distinction matters: without field boundaries, different input sequences
can have the same concatenated bytes. The helper orders fields, serializes one
unambiguous record and hashes its complete bytes.

The settings fix eight BPE merges; decoder width, feed-forward width and context
capacity of four; one attention head and one block; stride one; training and
evaluation batch sizes of sixteen and one hundred twenty-eight; thirty-two
updates; learning rate $0.04$; gradient-norm cap $1$; training seed $39$;
generation seed $38$; bigram smoothing $1$; generation temperature $0.8$;
top-k four; and three generated tokens. The identity records floating-point
settings by their exact bit patterns rather than rounded display text.

<RustSource path="rust/demos/practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff/src/lib.rs" region="reference-input-identity" caption="Bind configuration, exact fixture bytes and verified scalar-reference source to one input identity." label="Rust source: canonical scalar-reference input identity" />

The example verifies its compiled reference-source evidence first. It then
rejects changed corpus or split bytes before training or checkpoint work.
Only accepted fixed inputs reach the existing pipeline. The wrapper calls that
pipeline once; the pipeline itself performs primary training and replay.

<RustSource path="rust/demos/practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff/src/lib.rs" region="reference-handoff" caption="Reject changed fixtures, run the unchanged scalar pipeline and retain only its checked observation." label="Rust source: fixed-fixture admission and scalar-reference execution" />

### What matching identities do not prove

A matching digest identifies the same canonical input record, subject to the
hash's collision-resistance assumption. It does not prove that the algorithm
is correct or that a new machine will reproduce every floating-point bit.

The source identity deliberately covers the forty first-course source files,
not the evolving practical crate, this chapter's reporting wrapper or interface. Toolchain, locked
dependencies and arithmetic environment are recorded separately. A matching
source digest is therefore not evidence that two execution environments match.
The temporary checkpoint path is also outside the input identity; changing
that path does not change the model's fixed inputs.

Likewise, exact checkpoint reload is narrower than complete job resumption.
This check does not restore every data cursor, in-flight operation or whole-job
continuation state. No laptop throughput is measured here.

{/* chapter-section:history */}

## History: reporting conditions and measuring variation

A language-model score without its input conditions and scope does not identify
what was evaluated or establish which capabilities were checked.

[Model Cards for Model Reporting](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993v2) was
presented in 2019. Mitchell and colleagues propose model documentation that
includes intended uses and evaluation conditions; a model card is not itself
proof of quality.

Model Cards describe evaluation conditions and intended uses; later fine-tuning
experiments study variation across initializations and data orders. Reporting
scope and measuring variation answer different questions.

In [Fine-Tuning Pretrained Language Models: Weight Initializations, Data Orders, and Early Stopping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06305v1),
published in 2020, Dodge and colleagues study fine-tuning variability associated
with initialization and data order for pretrained language models. This does
not measure variability in the course's tiny decoder.

Keep a fixed regression reference when changing an LLM pipeline, while recording
separately the evidence needed for quality, seed sensitivity and hardware claims.

The Rust reporting contrast uses the same observation. Reading only the mean
NLL with this expression gives a number:

```rust
trace
    .observation()
    .final_evaluation()
    .decoder()
    .mean_nll()
```

`trace.report()` also states the evaluation unit, input identity, replay
accounting and limits. It does not retrain a historical model or execute a seed
sweep.

<RustSource path="rust/demos/practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff/src/lib.rs" region="scope-bearing-report" caption="Report the same scalar observation with its metric unit, input identity and explicit capability limits." label="Rust source: scope-bearing scalar-reference report" />

Repeating seed $39$ checks repeatability under fixed conditions. It does not
estimate variability across seeds. Those are complementary checks, not
interchangeable evidence.

{/* chapter-section:rust-implementation */}

## Run the reference without changing its inputs

The example obtains verified source evidence and owns its temporary checkpoint
location. Its report comes directly from the checked scalar observation, not
from parsing a previous human-readable report.

<RustSource path="rust/demos/practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff/src/main.rs" region="reference-example" caption="Verify the reference source, use an owned temporary checkpoint and print the scope-bearing report." label="Rust source: executable fixed scalar-reference example" />

{/* chapter-section:visualization */}

## Keep the three evidence layers separate

The digest identifies the fixed inputs. The counts and generated token IDs
describe checked behavior on those inputs. The final card keeps future quality,
job-resumption and hardware claims outside the reference's evidence boundary.

<ReferenceCoreHandoffDiagram labels={diagramLabels} />

{/* chapter-section:exercises */}

## Optional practice: inspect the boundary

From the repository root, with Docker and the Rust/site course image available,
run the example and inspect its JSON report:

```sh
COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo run --quiet --offline --locked -p practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff
```

The output contains the fixed input identity and the checked scalar-reference
observations described in this chapter.

1. In the JSON report printed by the Chapter 1 reference example, find the input
   identity, target-count basis and metric unit. Explain why a digest alone would
   not replace the replay and reload checks.
2. Run the pure identity-input mutation test. Identify its changes to configuration,
   corpus, split bytes and source identity without training. Explain why constructing
   an identity for changed inputs does not admit them to the fixed reference run.

   From the repository root, with Docker and the Rust/site course image available,
   run:

   ```sh
   COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff --test reference_handoff every_identity_input_is_bound_without_training -- --exact
   ```

   Expected result: one selected test passes. A zero-test result does not
   reproduce this check.

3. Explain why a successful checkpoint round trip cannot justify the statement
   “the complete training job can resume,” and why $1744$ must not be labeled
   “distinct test transitions.”

<details>
<summary>Answers: input identity, evidence scope and repeated target slots</summary>

1. The digest binds inputs; replay and reload compare actual behavior. Neither
   kind of evidence substitutes for the other. The target-count basis explicitly
   derives $2048$ targets per schedule and $4096$ for primary plus replay.
   The reported mean NLL uses nats per overlapping window-target slot.
2. The pure mutation test constructs different identities without calling the
   pipeline. The runner separately requires the exact accepted corpus and split
   bytes, so an identity is not an admission permit.
3. The checkpoint check covers persisted model, optimizer and tokenizer state
   plus a fixed logit probe, not every whole-job continuation dependency. The
   $1744$ denominator counts overlapping window-target slots; the underlying
   documents contain $442$ transition occurrences.

</details>

{/* chapter-section:decoder-connection */}

## What the next extension must preserve

You now have an identified scalar reference and a precisely bounded report.
A later change can be compared with that reference, while carrying its own
input identity and evidence. Chapter 2 uses NVIDIA NeMo Curator to prepare
supplied text, then loads the prepared documents through the practical crate's
Rust reader.
New data, larger models, accelerator execution, quality evaluation and complete
job resumption each require their own checks; none is already established by
this handoff.

import RustSource from "../../../components/RustSource.astro";
import CorpusPreparationDiagram from "../../../components/chapters/CorpusPreparationDiagram.astro";

{/* chapter-section:worked-example */}

## The problem: the model learns from the text we let through

A language model learns to predict tokens from the documents supplied during
training. Its optimizer does not decide whether those documents are appropriate
for the task, whether we may use them, or whether a purportedly unseen test
example also appears in the training input. Those decisions must happen before
training.

Repeated text creates another problem. If one training pass visits every stored
document occurrence, each copy of a document supplies another copy of its token
targets. The repeated text receives more influence without adding new examples.
Removing duplicates changes that weighting; it does not merely save disk space.

Corpus preparation therefore has two outputs: selected text and evidence about
how it was selected. We need source context, declared exclusion rules, duplicate
handling and protected evaluation boundaries. A large file or a successful
download supplies none of those conclusions on its own.

We will use [NVIDIA NeMo Curator](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/curator/v26.07/curate-text)
to prepare text. It is an external tool, not
part of the Rust language model, and another preparation tool can replace it if
it produces the same documented input for the model. Rust will only load the
prepared documents. The extended tokenizer in Chapter 3 will then learn from the
training documents, not the validation or test documents.

## The solution: prepare documents, then load a stable format

Keep one document as one record throughout the preparation pipeline. Retain a
stable document ID and the source information needed to trace that record. A
source record should identify where the text came from, its revision and the
applicable license and attribution. A checksum identifies selected bytes; it
does not establish permission to use those bytes or tell us what they contain.

Apply declared quality rules, inspect what those rules exclude, and handle
duplicates before final training input is frozen. Quality rules are proxies:
for example, a minimum word count rejects short records, not every unsuitable
record. A rule can also remove useful text. Inspect both survivors and exclusions
rather than interpreting a low exclusion rate as success.

Keep privacy review separate from quality scoring. Passing a word-count filter
or removing duplicates does not remove names, addresses, credentials or other
sensitive content. Withhold unresolved records from training; do not copy their
sensitive text into public reports. Retain enough source and transformation
information to identify affected derived corpora if an input is withdrawn.
Removing a source from a later corpus does not erase what an already trained
model may have learned from it.

### A six-document example

The practical example uses course-authored text, not a result for a large
training corpus. Its JSONL input contains these six documents:

| Document ID | Text | Source group | Relevant observation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `story-a` | A cat naps. | `family-a` | Three words |
| `story-b` | A cat naps. | `family-a` | An identical copy of `story-a` |
| `story-c` | A dog runs. | `family-b` | Three words |
| `story-d` | Rain feeds trees. | `family-c` | Three words |
| `story-e` | hi | `family-e` | One word |
| `story-f` | !!! | `family-f` | Punctuation only |

Configure NeMo's word-count filter to retain records with at least $3$ and at
most $20$ words. Its English setting counts whitespace-separated items; that
proxy is not a linguistic definition of a word. The $4$ story occurrences
survive; `hi` and the punctuation-only
record do not. Exact duplicate removal then leaves $3$ distinct story texts.
The punctuation-only record has one whitespace-separated item too; this
particular rule rejects it for length, not because it recognizes punctuation
as unsuitable language-model training text.
The duplicate-removal workflow may retain either cat-story ID; the result we
care about here is one cat-story occurrence, not a promised representative ID
or output-file order.

Before deduplication, the cat story occupies $2$ of the $4$ surviving document
occurrences. After deduplication, it occupies $1$ of $3$ distinct documents. Under
uniform sampling of these whole-stage document occurrences before separating
their roles, its selection probability would change from $2/4$ to $1/3$.
That calculation illustrates duplicate weighting, not a sampler used to train
on this fixture. Actual token-target weighting also depends on document length,
split selection and the batching policy; document fractions are not token
fractions.

NeMo's exact method groups hashes of text and identifies copies to remove.
It does not identify paraphrases, and hash grouping is not an adversarial
collision-proof comparison. NeMo's fuzzy method uses approximate similarity
search for near-duplicates. Its configuration trades missed matches against
unwanted matches; it does not certify a universal similarity cutoff or detect
all ways an evaluation example could have leaked into training.

### Freeze the roles of the prepared documents

The training split supplies examples for fitting the tokenizer and model.
The validation split supplies examples for selecting settings or deciding when
to stop training. The test split is reserved for final evaluation. Do not move
a difficult held-out document into training after seeing its score.

Related records must not be scattered across those roles. Treat an identified
duplicate family or other known related source group as one unit when assigning
splits. Otherwise two different IDs can put substantially the same example in
both training and evaluation. For this fixture, the two cat-story copies share
`family-a`; their different IDs do not make them independent examples.

For the exercise, a supplied policy assigns `family-a`, `family-e` and
`family-f` to training, `family-b` to validation and `family-c` to test. We fix
that policy before running the filters. Both cat-story copies therefore have
the same role regardless of which ID duplicate removal keeps. The prepared
fixture has one document in each role: the cat story in training, the dog story
in validation and the rain story in test.

The recipe uses Pandas to join those declared assignments to the source-group
metadata. It refuses an unassigned group rather than choosing a convenient role
after seeing the output. This checks the supplied groups, not whether we have
discovered every related pair. One held-out story is also far too little
evidence for a meaningful model-quality estimate.

Split disjointness and decontamination are different checks. Disjoint IDs do not
prove different text. Removing exact duplicates does not prove that near-copies
or external benchmark examples are absent. Declare the protected evaluation
material and the overlap method before inspecting results, report its measured
scope, and keep unresolved overlaps out of training. A check against a named
evaluation set does not establish internet-wide contamination freedom.

### Export documents, not preparation-specific objects

The handoff to Rust is UTF-8 **JSON Lines**: one JSON object per physical line.
Each object has a nonblank string `id` and a nonblank string `text`. Other fields
are retained as metadata. For example:

```json
{"id":"story-c","text":"A dog runs.","source_group":"family-b"}
```

The document ID is a label, not a token ID or a required filename. The text is
still text; tokenization comes next. A newline inside document text must be
escaped as `\n` inside the JSON string, so it does not create a second record.
Source and split records remain linked to the exported documents, but a JSONL
file alone does not certify that those decisions were made correctly.

{/* chapter-section:formula */}

## Formula: distinguish retention from quality

For a nonempty input corpus, the final document-retention fraction is

$$
r_{\mathrm{keep}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{prepared}}}{N_{\mathrm{input}}}
$$

{/* chapter-section:symbol-glossary */}

Here $N_{\mathrm{input}}$ is the number of input document occurrences,
$N_{\mathrm{prepared}}$ is the number remaining after the declared preparation
stages, and $r_{\mathrm{keep}}$ is a dimensionless fraction. Neither count is a
byte count or token count. With zero input documents, the fraction is undefined;
report that condition rather than inventing a zero-quality score.

In the six-document example, quality filtering retains $4/6$ of the original
input. Duplicate removal retains $3/4$ of its own input: the four records that
reached that stage. Their product is the final retention fraction,

$$
\frac{4}{6}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Changing the denominator changes the question. Reporting $1/6$ as the duplicate
stage's exclusion fraction would use the original input population rather than
the $4$ records the duplicate stage examined. Keep every stage's entering and
leaving document counts so its fraction can be interpreted locally.

Keeping half the input says how much remains under this policy. It does not say
that half was bad, that the survivors are safe, or that a model trained on them
will perform well. Those claims need different evidence.

## Practical preparation with NeMo Curator

This workflow uses a separately built NeMo Curator image. You need Linux,
Docker, a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so
Docker can expose the GPU. The pinned NeMo release must be compatible with that
CUDA/driver stack. Rust's prepared-corpus reader does not require a GPU or CUDA.

Run the following commands from the repository root. The image build may use
network access to obtain the external tool. It does not acquire a training
corpus or add NeMo to the Rust/site image:

```sh
docker build --file docker/nemo-curator.Dockerfile \
  --tag learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 .
```

With the NeMo image built and the NVIDIA GPU available to Docker, run from the
repository root. Create a fresh output directory for the exercise, then run the
tool with network access disabled. The read-only mount supplies the recipe and
its six-record fixture; the writable mount receives generated preparation output:

```sh
mkdir -p .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture
docker run --rm --network none --gpus all --memory=8g --cpus=2 --shm-size=1g \
  --hostname course-nemo --add-host course-nemo:127.0.0.1 \
  --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/tools/nemo-curator",target=/course,readonly \
  --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/.build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture",target=/output \
  learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 \
  /course/prepare_corpus.py \
    --input /course/fixtures/raw.jsonl --output /output \
    --split-policy /course/fixtures/splits.json
```

Use an empty output directory. If the directory already contains an earlier
attempt, choose a different directory rather than overwriting its evidence.
The hostname mapping lets the local Ray workers resolve their container on
loopback; it does not enable external network access.

The recipe invokes NeMo's reader, configured word-count filter, exact duplicate
identification and duplicate-removal workflow. Identification produces IDs to
remove; it is not already the prepared text. The removal workflow must consume
those IDs from the same input and ID policy, then export the remaining documents.

The filter configuration in `tools/nemo-curator/prepare_corpus.py` uses the
library's pipeline and stages; the recipe does not implement its own filter:

```python
Pipeline(
    name="course_corpus_quality",
    stages=[
        JsonlReader(file_paths=str(input_path), read_kwargs=read_kwargs),
        ScoreFilter(
            filter_obj=WordCountFilter(min_words=min_words, max_words=max_words, lang="en"),
            score_field="word_count",
        ),
        JsonlWriter(path=str(quality_path), mode="error"),
    ],
).run(executor=executor)
```

The surrounding recipe supplies the reader settings, starts a local Ray client,
and runs NeMo's exact-identification and text-removal workflows. The defaults
set `min_words` to `3` and `max_words` to `20`. Command-line options change those
values; retain them with the output report when comparing different policies.
The supplied split-policy file is independent of the observed scores.

Inspect the generated report and exported files with these commands, still from
the repository root:

```sh
cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/report.json
cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/prepared.jsonl
cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/train.jsonl
```

For this fixture, the expected
stage counts are $6$ input documents, $4$ after word-count filtering and $3$ after
exact duplicate removal. The final texts are `A cat naps.`, `A dog runs.` and
`Rain feeds trees.`; do not require one particular cat-story ID. The report also
records one document in each role. `prepared.jsonl` contains all three documents
for inspection; `train.jsonl`, `validation.jsonl` and `test.jsonl` contain their
respective selections and retain the `split` metadata.

This is a tiny execution example with a fixed assignment of known source
groups. It is not an approval of a larger corpus, a privacy check, proof that all
related groups were found or a trained-model result. The helper limits input to
$4$ MiB and $4096$ documents by default so the example is inspectable; those are
not a recipe for processing the previously acquired large corpus. A bulk run
needs its own feasible configuration and complete selection evidence.

For a real corpus, also retain input provenance, the tool version and configuration,
excluded-document counts, the duplicate policy, split assignments and the scope
of overlap and privacy review. A successful small fixture does not establish
that the same resource settings fit a larger dataset. Select and measure that
workload separately, preserving the raw inputs and every failed attempt.

{/* chapter-section:rust-implementation */}

## Load the prepared output in Rust

`PreparedCorpusReader` accepts any caller-supplied `BufRead` stream. A file,
memory buffer or database export can supply that stream without changing the
loader. Standard buffered I/O reads physical lines; Serde JSON parses their
objects. The loader preserves decoded text and metadata. It does not normalize
text, reject duplicate content or assign a split.

<RustSource
  path="rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs"
  region="prepared-document-json"
  caption="The prepared-corpus loader uses Serde JSON to decode required document fields, then rejects blank IDs or text without rewriting their content."
  label="Rust source: decode one prepared document without curating it"
/>

The caller chooses maximum source-record bytes, document count and cumulative
decoded-text bytes. Record bytes include the physical line ending; decoded text
bytes count the UTF-8 representation of the `text` value, not JSON syntax or
metadata. An oversized record, malformed JSON, missing required field, failed
read or exceeded limit stops the stream with an error. No failed document is
returned or counted. Documents returned earlier are not rolled back.

<RustSource
  path="rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs"
  region="prepared-corpus-stream"
  caption="The prepared-corpus iterator stops after successful end of input or its first error; it never resumes past a failed record."
  label="Rust source: stop the prepared-document stream at its error boundary"
/>

The demo reads standard input, retains only the first three document descriptions
for its summary, and emits that summary only after the complete input succeeds.
It can therefore inspect a large stream without retaining every text. This is
not a transactional storage adapter: a caller storing documents as they arrive
must provide its own staging if partial results must stay unpublished.

<RustSource
  path="rust/demos/practical-ch02-corpus-preparation/src/lib.rs"
  region="load-prepared-corpus"
  caption="The Rust demo loads supplied prepared documents, reports their count and decoded text bytes, and does not repeat NeMo's preparation operations."
  label="Rust source: summarize a caller-supplied prepared corpus"
/>

With Docker running and the Rust workspace image available, load the output from
the preceding NeMo command. Run from the repository root:

```sh
COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo run --offline --locked \
  -p practical-ch02-corpus-preparation \
```

{/* chapter-section:history */}

## History: more text was not the whole solution

Collecting readable text alone does not document its intended use, control the
weight of repeated occurrences or protect held-out evaluation from training
overlap.

Dataset documentation makes source context reviewable; deduplication studies
connect repeated training text with memorization and train-test overlap in
their measured settings.

[Datasheets for Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010v8) was first posted in
$2018$. Gebru and colleagues propose documenting dataset motivation,
composition, collection and intended uses so those choices can be reviewed.
Documentation records context; it does not itself establish permission or
privacy.

The $2021$ [C4 analysis](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.98/) examined
where web-corpus text came from and what filtering removed. Its finding that
blocklist filtering disproportionately excluded text from and about minority
individuals is a reason to inspect exclusions, not to label every filter neutral.

In $2022$, [Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better](https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.577/)
studied duplicate handling in training corpora. Lee and colleagues report reduced memorized output and train-test
overlap after deduplication in their studied corpora and models; those outcomes
are not measurements of this course fixture. They explain why duplicate
handling and evaluation separation matter in addition to collecting and
documenting text.

The following Rust comparison loads two identical supplied records and keeps
both. It illustrates the limitation of merely reading raw occurrences, not a
reimplementation of those studies' preparation tools:

<RustSource
  path="rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs"
  region="loading-is-not-preparation"
  caption="Reading two identical JSONL records returns two documents; the loader does not silently perform duplicate removal."
  label="Rust comparison: loading records does not prepare a corpus"
/>

Keep documented source and selection evidence, inspect exclusions, handle
related records together and preserve held-out roles before tokenizer learning
or model training. No single preparation statistic certifies suitability.

{/* chapter-section:visualization */}

## Follow the preparation-to-learning boundary

<CorpusPreparationDiagram />

The preparation tool owns the configured exclusions and duplicate handling.
The exported documents and their source and split evidence cross the boundary
into the Rust training pipeline. The Rust loader reads that selection; the
tokenizer learns only from the training role. Passing a record between stages
does not grant it a new quality or privacy guarantee.

{/* chapter-section:exercises */}

## Optional practice: reproduce and explain the boundary

1. Load the manually prepared fixture with the first command below. Explain
   why matching its counts to the NeMo output does not identify its producer
   or establish that its text is suitable for training.
2. Run the malformed-later-input test with the second command. Explain what
   happens to the success summary and to the document returned before the error.

Run these commands from the repository root with Docker running. The supplied
JSONL file is a separate, manually prepared course fixture; it is not a substitute
for the preceding NeMo execution.

```sh
COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo run --offline --locked \
  -p practical-ch02-corpus-preparation \
  < rust/demos/practical-ch02-corpus-preparation/fixtures/prepared.jsonl
```

This command also prints $3$ loaded documents and $39$ decoded text bytes. Explain
why equal counts do not prove that NeMo produced this file or that its content
is suitable for training.

From the repository root, with Docker running and the Rust workspace image
available, reproduce the loader's failure boundary:

```sh
COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked \
  -p practical-ch02-corpus-preparation --lib \
  tests::malformed_later_input_has_no_success_summary -- --exact
```

The test should report `running 1 test` and `1 passed; 0 failed`. It supplies one
valid document followed by malformed JSON and confirms that the demo produces no
success summary. Zero selected tests means this check did not run.

<details>
<summary>Explanations for the prepared-corpus loading tasks</summary>

1. The manually prepared fixture has its own origin. Matching its document and
   byte counts to the NeMo example checks only those quantities, not its producer,
   selection policy, source rights, privacy or split assignment. Keep the actual
   NeMo input, configuration and output evidence when reproducing that workflow.

2. For malformed later input, the iterator has already returned the earlier valid
   document before it encounters the error. The demo withholds its final success
   summary because it consumes the stream completely before printing. A different
   caller that wrote each returned document immediately would need its own staging
   to prevent partial publication.

</details>

{/* chapter-section:decoder-connection */}

## What reaches the language model next

Prepared training documents become the tokenizer's learning input in Chapter 3.
Held-out documents may be encoded with the learned tokenizer, but they must not
change its learned vocabulary or merge choices. Later batching creates token
targets from that same frozen training selection. NeMo has not implemented any
of those Rust LLM algorithms; it has supplied documented text for them to learn
from.

{
  "chapter_id": "02-corpus-preparation",
  "locale": "en",
  "title": "Corpus preparation",
  "description": "Terms for selecting training text, handling repeated examples, protecting evaluation roles and reading prepared documents.",
  "terms": [
    {"term": "Training corpus", "definition": "The selected documents that supply examples for tokenizer learning and model training, together with evidence of their source and preparation policy."},
    {"term": "Document occurrence", "definition": "One stored instance of a document. Two records containing the same text are two occurrences and can give that text extra training weight."},
    {"term": "Retention fraction", "definition": "Prepared-document count divided by input-document count for a nonempty input. It measures how much the declared pipeline retains, not the quality of its survivors."},
    {"term": "Exact deduplication", "definition": "Remove repeated text under a declared equality policy. The NeMo example groups text hashes and keeps one representative; it does not detect paraphrases or certify collision-proof equality."},
    {"term": "Near-duplicate", "definition": "A document sufficiently similar to another under a declared matching method. Approximate searches can miss related text or group text that should remain distinct."},
    {"term": "Source group", "definition": "Records declared to belong to one related source family. The exercise assigns each supplied group to a single split; that assignment does not prove all related records were discovered."},
    {"term": "Held-out split", "definition": "Validation or test documents kept out of tokenizer learning and model fitting. Validation informs setting choices; test evaluation is reserved for the final assessment."},
    {"term": "Decontamination", "definition": "Check and exclude training overlap with declared protected evaluation material using a specified method. Passing that check does not establish absence of every possible leak."},
    {"term": "Prepared-document interchange", "definition": "UTF-8 JSONL records with nonblank string id and text fields and retained metadata. Rust loads the supplied selection without redoing filtering, duplicate removal or split assignment."}
  ]
}
